definition: Placate means to ease the anger of, soothe.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word placate. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know placate should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A tray of free samples at the door did little to placate the neighbors after the bakery's mixers ran all night.
Calm is the mildest and most general word here — you can calm a nervous friend who isn't angry at anyone at all, while you placate someone whose anger is aimed squarely at you.
Appease goes further than calm or placate—the appeaser pays for quiet, granting the angry side what it demands and hoping the bill stops there.

Conciliate aims past the outburst at the relationship itself — a conciliating manager wants the two sides working together again, not merely quiet. Placate has the narrower job of taking the heat out of someone's present anger, usually with a gesture. You placate to end a scene; you conciliate to mend the bond.

Mollify means to soften someone's anger, often only partly — a small apology mollifies without fully satisfying. Placate is more transactional: a concrete gesture — the free dessert, the comped repair — offered so the anger will stand down. Mollify takes the edge off the mood; placate answers the grievance with amends.

When the venue moved the concert indoors at the last minute, the promoter tried to placate furious ticket holders with front-row upgrades and signed posters—an hour later the line at the refund window had thinned to nothing.
Placate points at a person's anger and works to lower it, usually with a gesture: the upgrade, the discount, the apology.
It is more targeted than 'calm'—you calm nerves or a crowd in any mood, but you placate someone who is angry at you.
Placate is the everyday verb for taking the heat out of someone's anger with a gesture.

Its unit-mates divide the work: assuage eases the feeling itself (you assuage anger, but placate the angry person); appease, in the reference list, is placate with the price paid in concessions; conciliate (a chip above) aims at repairing the whole relationship.
If no one is actually angry, you want 'calm,' not placate.

The wave pool shut down without warning on the hottest Saturday of July, stranding a snaking line of families in the sun.
Within minutes, guests were chanting for refunds, and one man demanded the manager's name three times.
Rosa, the shift lead, had thirty seconds to decide how to placate a crowd that was only getting louder.
She sent staff down the line with cold water, free ice cream bars, and same-day passes to every other attraction.
The chanting faded to grumbling, then to the ordinary noise of a busy park; the complaints, Rosa knew, were paused rather than solved, but the afternoon was saved.
